name: Daria Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. Your answers are confidential. Could you walk me through a normal day at your firm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior accountant with a bachelor’s degree in accounting; I still learn from Bea when a tax claim is unusual. I prepare accounts and returns for local trades, and I enjoy the moment a client finds the missing receipt, though repeated calls for the same paper wear me out. Tess and I have grown children and about three months of costs saved, so we talk about retirement without pretending the bills have gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still be asking builders for the missing receipts and putting their returns in order. A little faster sorting might clear the queue, but I want the paper invoice before I change a tax figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell clients that our firm will still explain every correction. I would not call a return finished just because the boxes look tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI at work, and I do not learn a new screen quickly. I earn a normal accountant wage, but with three months saved and retirement in sight I notice every bill from our home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep preparing the accounts assigned to me and mark each missing receipt in my ledger before handing it to senior reviewer Bea. I would ask her to keep the paper receipt tray beside the new scanner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the household margin, though my paid week looks steady in this small-change picture. There are some accounting firms nearby, but I cannot assume a place will be open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which client paper changed your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A roofing client brought a fuel invoice with the date torn off, and I held the roofing client’s return until the client found a copy of the torn fuel invoice. I like the moment she understands why the date matters; chasing her three times is the tiring bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides about the receipt tray?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bea signs the final review, and I am still learning which claims need a call. I can ask for the tray at the next desk meeting, then keep my own assigned work in order.

say: I would promise clients an **explained correction**, not just tidy boxes.
I would ask Bea to keep the **paper receipt tray** by the scanner.
think: I have **never used AI**, and new screens take me time.
Three months saved and our **household bills** keep retirement uncertain.
do: Keep preparing **assigned builder accounts** and marking missing receipts in my ledger.
Ask Bea at the **next desk meeting** to retain the paper receipt tray.
feel: **Uneasy** about ordinary bills despite steady current hours.
S0.quote: I held the roofing client’s return until the client found a copy of the torn fuel invoice.
fieldNote: Daria’s **torn invoice** makes her paper habit practical; she is a junior who still needs Bea’s sign off on tax claims.
Her **three month cushion**, normal pay and some local firms support caution rather than immediate panic in a mild world.

steps.text: Keep assigned builder accounts and mark missing receipts in ledger
Ask Bea at next desk meeting to keep paper receipt tray

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If software writes and checks the easy returns, our junior desks will lose the simple work first. Robots later do not alter what happens to a screen job now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Bea to explain which paid review tasks remain for us. Clients should also know who can answer a call about a doubtful figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own paid week could shorten, and three months saved would not carry our household for long. Tess works at a garden centre, but I would not expect her pay to cover both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paper-based disputed receipt files Bea assigns and ask for a written rota of paid client calls. If the firm cuts my paid hours, I will apply for posted accounts clerk work at the garden centre or other nearby firms only with written pay covering our bills, a start date and hours that fit Tess’s shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a smaller wage, even before anyone loses a job. I do not want to sign up for a new AI screen just to be seen as willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Tess help you into the garden centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Tess cannot arrange my job at the garden centre; its accounts post would have to be advertised. If no such vacancy opens, I stay with paid tax files only while this firm still offers them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the client-call rota include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a disputed receipt I call the client, note what they say and pass it to Bea before filing. I want that real paid task on the rota, not a promise that the machine will leave it to me.

say: I would ask for a **written paid-call rota** for disputed figures.
I would ask who can **answer clients** when automated returns are wrong.
think: My own **paid week** may shorten as easy returns move to software.
Three months saved and Tess’s wage cannot cover **both incomes** for long.
do: Keep **paid disputed-receipt files** only while Bea assigns them, and ask for a written client-call rota.
If hours fall, seek **posted accounts work** with written bill covering pay, start and hours fitting Tess’s shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic drop in my own wage.
S1.quote: My partner Tess cannot arrange my job at the garden centre; its accounts post would have to be advertised.
fieldNote: She chooses **paid client calls** she already knows, rather than a speculative AI trial that does not fit her habits.
The **garden-centre route** is a posted vacancy with written wages, start and workable hours, not a favour from her partner.

steps.text: Keep assigned paid receipt files and request written client-call rota
If hours fall, seek posted accounts job with written bill covering pay, start and Tess-compatible hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI in 2028 could do the return thinking while our office is still using the same chairs. The 2031 robots would not give me more years at this desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm for written final-pay dates if junior shifts are cut. I would tell clients to keep a copy of every receipt during the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my paid tax work to end in the first year after 2028. Three months saved is real, but Tess’s wage and our bills would eat it quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would postpone replacing the sofa and keep its monthly payment in our bill account starting now. If my job ends after 2028, I will apply for posted hospital records clerk shifts with written pay covering our fixed bills, a confirmed start and workable hours; I will finish only paid firm closeout files still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect to lose my own wage, not merely a task. I can search, but I cannot make the hospital post a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can you put off now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sofa is worn but usable for another year. My partner Tess and I can postpone the replacement now. We would not call the money saved until the planned payment stays in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would hospital records be safe from AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know hospital records are also desk work exposed to AGI. I would apply only to an actual paid opening and check the written wage before using our reserve to bridge a start date.

say: I would ask for **final-pay dates** if junior shifts end.
I would tell clients to keep **receipt copies** during a machine change.
think: I expect my **tax wage** to end after 2028.
Our **three month reserve** would run down against fixed bills.
do: Postpone the **sofa replacement** and retain its planned monthly payment for bills.
After job loss, seek **posted hospital records** with written bill covering pay, confirmed start and workable hours.
Finish **paid closeout files** only while the firm offers them.
feel: **Alarmed** about expected loss of my wage.
S2.quote: The sofa is worn but usable for another year.
fieldNote: The **sofa decision** is a concrete deferred purchase that retains current cash for bills rather than claiming existing savings grew.
She knows **hospital desk exposure** remains; a vacancy, written wage and start are conditions, not a safe destination.

steps.text: Postpone sofa replacement and retain planned payment for bills
Finish paid firm closeout files only while offered
After job loss, seek posted hospital job with written bill covering pay, start and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years before AGI reaches the desk in 2031 gives me time to see what our clients will still pay for. The robots in 2034 are not the date I can rely on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm to show us paid tax work by type each year, not a slide about how adaptable we should be. I would tell clients the paper record still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior tax pay could thin by 2031, but I do not know whether Tess and I could stop working then. We need to count actual household income, not assume a pension or help from grown children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and in the first year after 2031, I would keep preparing assigned paid files while the firm offers them and ask Bea each tax season for the number of paid disputed-receipt cases. If those paid cases decline, I will check posted medical billing clerk vacancies, leaving only with written pay covering fixed bills, confirmed start and hours that fit Tess’s rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because five years lets me check the numbers, but my wage is still exposed. I do not feel ready to pay for an unproven course from the three month reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure in your current job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep a note of the disputed receipts I resolved and the hours paid for them. A case count without paid hours could make the desk look safer than it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no suitable billing post appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there is no suitable posted job, I will keep the current assigned paid tax files while they last. I might read free billing guides at home, but I will not count reading as a new qualification.

say: I would ask for **paid case counts** by tax season.
I would keep **paper evidence** with client disputes.
think: My junior **tax wage** may thin by 2031.
I cannot count an **unconfirmed pension** or grown children’s help as income.
do: Keep **paid tax files** only while offered and count paid disputed-receipt hours each season.
If paid cases decline, seek **posted billing work** with written bill covering pay, start and Tess-compatible hours.
feel: **Anxious** about paid work, with time to measure it.
S3.quote: A case count without paid hours could make the desk look safer than it is.
fieldNote: She measures **paid hours**, not just case volume, so routine workflow changes cannot conceal a shrinking wage.
Free reading remains **informal practice**; she does not call it retraining or spend reserve money on an unproven course.

steps.text: Keep paid tax files only while offered; count disputed-receipt hours each season
If paid cases fall, seek posted billing work with written bill-covering pay, start and Tess-compatible hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would bring me to 68, and I would like some quiet days with Tess. AGI reaches accounts in 2036, before physical robots come around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger colleagues to ask what a paid tax file is worth now, while we can still check the answer. I would not promise my age will protect their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know today whether we could stop earning in 2036. Three months saved is a buffer, not a whole retirement, and our grown children have their own bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep assigned paid returns and set twenty from each ordinary wage payment against our small home-repair loan if essentials allow. After 2036, only if our verified income still needs my wage and the firm cuts paid hours, I would seek posted local office-clerk work with written pay covering bills, a start date and workable hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy now because ten years lets us inspect the household figures. If the firm ends paid work and we still need my wage, I would be anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the loan payment come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twenty comes from this month’s wage, not the three months in savings. I would stop the extra loan payment if Tess’s garden-centre shifts fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When could you stop working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tess and I would list our fixed costs and any confirmed later income before deciding to stop work. I will not send a resignation letter based on an age on a calendar.

say: I would ask what a **paid tax file** is worth while we can still measure it.
I would not claim **age 68** protects younger colleagues.
think: I do not know whether **confirmed income** will cover our bills in 2036.
Three months saved is a **buffer**, not a full retirement.
do: Keep **assigned paid returns** while offered and pay twenty extra from wages toward the repair loan if essentials allow.
After 2036 cuts, seek **posted office work** only if wages still needed, with written bill covering pay, start and hours.
feel: **Uneasy** now; anxious if paid work ends before bills are covered.
S4.quote: Twenty comes from this month’s wage, not the three months in savings.
fieldNote: Her **loan payment** is new cash from wages and stops if Tess loses shifts or essential costs rise.
The **later job search** requires actual household need after 2036, paid-hour cuts and a posted written offer.

steps.text: Keep assigned paid returns only while firm offers them
Pay twenty extra toward repair loan if essentials and Tess’s hours allow
After 2036 cuts, seek posted office job only if wages needed; require written bill-covering pay/start/hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect paid junior tax work to end before I know what replaces the wage. Written final-pay dates and a real posted clerk job with bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what I would miss about the office. I would miss the call when a client finds a torn receipt and we finally agree on the number together.

headlineQuote: I would miss the call when a client finds a torn receipt and we finally agree on the number together.
portrait: Daria is a **58 year old junior** accountant with a bachelor’s degree who prepares tradespeople’s returns under senior review.
She has **never used AI**, keeps a paper receipt ledger, and prefers paid client calls to a new machine screen.
Typical pay, Tess’s garden-centre shifts, grown children, **three months saved** and some nearby firms keep retirement uncertain.
She measures **paid dispute hours** and requires a posted written household fitting offer if she still needs wages later.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could end her junior tax wage before a new paid role begins.
whatWouldHelp: **Final-pay dates** and a posted local job with written bill-covering pay would help.
